title: Thinking Out of Order: When Output Order Stops Reflecting Reasoning Order in Diffusion Language Models

paper.title: Thinking Out of Order: When Output Order Stops Reflecting Reasoning Order in Diffusion Language Models
paper.abstract:
Abstract Autoregressive (AR) language models enforce a fixed left-to-right generation order, creating a fundamental limitation when the required output structure conflicts with natural reasoning (e.g., producing answers before explanations due to presentation or schema constraints). In such cases, AR models must commit to answers before generating intermediate reasoning, and this rigid constraint forces premature commitment. Masked diffusion language models (MDLMs), which iteratively refine all tokens in parallel, offer a way to decouple computation order from output structure.
We validate this capability on GSM8K, Math500, and ReasonOrderQA, a benchmark we introduce with controlled difficulty and order-level evaluation. When prompts request answers before reasoning, AR models exhibit large accuracy gaps compared to standard chain-of-thought ordering (up to 67% relative drop), while MDLMs remain stable ( ≤ \leq 14% relative drop), a property we term order robustness .
Using ReasonOrderQA, we present evidence that MDLMs achieve order robustness by stabilizing simpler tokens (e.g., reasoning steps) earlier in the diffusion process than complex ones (e.g., final answers), enabling reasoning tokens to stabilize before answer commitment. Finally, we identify failure conditions where this advantage weakens, outlining the limits required for order robustness.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Figure 1 : Masked Diffusion models reason before answering—even when asked to answer first. Under “answer-first” prompting, AR models must commit to answers before reasoning (generation order = output order). Masked diffusion LMs decode reasoning tokens first regardless of output position, enabling order robustness . Instruction-following is a fundamental capability of modern language models, enabling them to adhere to user-specified constraints on output format and structure ( Ouyang et al., 2022 ; Wei et al., 2021 ) . Chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting ( Kojima et al., 2022 ; Wei et al., 2022 ) extends this capability to complex reasoning tasks by instructing models to generate intermediate reasoning steps before producing final answers, significantly improving performance across diverse domains. However, this success depends on a critical assumption: the output order aligns with the model’s internal reasoning order. In practice, this assumption is often violated by deployment constraints that prioritize application needs, such as the Minto Pyramid principle ( Minto, 2009 ) mandating conclusions before arguments to optimize human comprehension, or JSON schemas ( Tam et al., 2024 ) enforcing fixed key sequences that force models to produce complex outputs (e.g., summary statistics) before the data needed to derive them. For autoregressive (AR) language models, this mismatch exposes a fundamental limitation of left-to-right generation. AR models factorize sequences strictly in temporal order ( Vaswani et al., 2017 ; Brown et al., 2020 ) , coupling the generation order (the sequence of probability assignments) with the output order (the sequence of emitted tokens). When answers must precede reasoning in the output, AR models are forced to commit to answer tokens before the intermediate reasoning tokens exist in the generated context. This premature commitment constrains the model’s ability to revise early predictions and has been shown to limit non-monotonic generation and bidirectional planning ( Welleck et al., 2019 ; Gu et al., 2019 ) . Yet its consequences for instruction-constrained reasoning remain largely unexplored. Masked diffusion language models (MDLMs) offer an alternative generation paradigm. Rather than producing tokens sequentially, MDLMs iteratively refine a full-length sequence using a bidirectional Transformer and a sampling procedure that determines which positions to finalize at each step ( Nie et al., 2025 ; Sahoo et al., 2024 ) . This process decouples computation order from textual position, allowing token estimates to evolve based on global sequence context and potentially enabling internal reasoning to emerge before answer commitment, even when answers appear first in the output. While recent work has primarily evaluated diffusion LMs in terms of final output quality and inference efficiency ( Wu et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2025b ) , their ability to support reliable reasoning under strict output-order constraints has not been systematically examined. To investigate this capability, we study order robustness , defined as the ability to maintain reasoning accuracy when the prompt-specified output order is reversed (CoT-First versus Answer-First). Across GSM8K, Math500, and a new benchmark we introduce, we uncover a striking contrast between generation paradigms. Under Answer-First prompting, Qwen ( Yang et al., 2024 ) (autoregressive) exhibits large relative accuracy drops (up to ∼ \sim 67%), whereas LLaDA ( Nie et al., 2025 ) (diffusion trained from scratch) remains largely stable with only a 4% relative drop. Dream ( Ye et al., 2025 ) , a diffusion model distilled from autoregressive weights, shows intermediate degradation ( ∼ \sim 46%), indicating that order robustness depends not only on architecture but also on training methodology. To make the underlying mechanism measurable rather than anecdotal, we introduce ReasonOrderQA , a controlled benchmark with graded arithmetic complexity (D1-D4) and explicit order-level evaluation. As illustrated in Figure 1 , we observe a consistent complexity-driven stabilization pattern in diffusion generation: lower-complexity reasoning tokens achieve high confidence and stabilize earlier than higher-complexity answer tokens, enabling internal reasoning to be refined before answer commitment regardless of output position. We further probe the boundaries of this mechanism and identify specific conditions under which order robustness breaks down. Our contributions: • We introduce ReasonOrderQA , a controlled benchmark with graded difficulty and order-level evaluation, enabling fine-grained analysis of order sensitivity across different token complexity levels. • Our detailed experiments provide evidence for order-robust reasoning in masked diffusion LMs: unlike AR models that degrade significantly under answer-first prompting, diffusion models maintain accuracy regardless of output order. • We systematically identify the mechanism for such order-robustness i.e. diffusion sampling automatically delays commitment on low-confidence tokens such as the final answers while high confidence tokens that convey reasoning stabilize earlier. • Finally, we identify failure cases where order robustness weakens, highlighting the limits of this implicit effect and identifying directions for reliable order-agnostic generation.

sections.heading: 2 Preliminary
sections.text: We define order robustness as the ability to maintain reasoning accuracy when the prompt-specified output order is altered (e.g., CoT-First vs. Answer-First).

sections.heading: Autoregressive Models.
sections.text: Autoregressive (AR) models factorize the joint probability of a sequence 𝐱 = [ x 1 , … , x L ] \mathbf{x}=[x_{1},\dots,x_{L}] as: p AR ​ ( 𝐱 ) = ∏ i = 1 L p ⁡ ( x i ∣ x < i ) p_{\text{AR}}(\mathbf{x})=\prod_{i=1}^{L}p(x_{i}\mid x_{<i}) (1) This enforces a strict left-to-right dependency: the prediction of token x i x_{i} can only attend to past context x < i x_{<i} , coupling generation order with textual position. Figure 2 : ReasonOrderQA benchmark design. Each problem contains (1) a noisy context with hidden variable definitions, (2) an arithmetic formula of varying complexity (D1-D4), and (3) evaluation under two generation orders (Standard: reasoning→answer, Reverse: answer→reasoning). This design decouples retrieval difficulty from reasoning complexity.

sections.heading: Masked Diffusion Language Models.
sections.text: Masked diffusion LMs like LLaDA ( Nie et al., 2025 ) define a reverse process that recovers clean data from a fully masked sequence. A bidirectional Transformer predicts all masked tokens simultaneously, allowing the model to access global context at any step and theoretically decoupling generation order from textual position. Starting from a fully masked sequence at step t = T t=T , the model iteratively predicts 𝐱 ^ 0 \hat{\mathbf{x}}_{0} from 𝐱 t \mathbf{x}_{t} . At each diffusion step, high-confidence tokens are retained while low-confidence tokens are re-masked for refinement in subsequent steps (i.e., tokens with low confidence are “remasked”). This prioritizes high-certainty predictions globally, regardless of their position in the sequence. We use this as our default strategy throughout the paper; alternative strategies are compared in § 6.3 .

sections.heading: Task Formulation and Metrics.
sections.text: To precisely analyze the generation dynamics, we formalize the task settings and define the terminology used throughout our experiments. We consider two output orders for a question x Q x_{Q} with rationale x R x_{R} and answer x A x_{A} . In the CoT-First setting, the model produces 𝐱 = [ x Q , x R , x A ] \mathbf{x}=[x_{Q},x_{R},x_{A}] , which matches the standard left-to-right reasoning narrative and the autoregressive training objective. In the Answer-First setting, the model is constrained to output 𝐱 = [ x Q , x A , x R ] \mathbf{x}=[x_{Q},x_{A},x_{R}] . The prompt templates enforcing these formats are provided in Appendix F .

sections.heading: Generation Settings.
sections.text: We use generation length L = 256 L=256 and diffusion steps T = 256 T=256 . Because the model estimates the entire sequence at every step, we can track internal predictions separately from the completion text (tokens actually committed). Full settings are in Appendix A (Table 4 ). Figure 3 : Order robustness across diffusion and autoregressive models. We compare LLaDA (diffusion, trained from scratch), Dream (diffusion, distilled from AR), and Qwen (autoregressive) on GSM8K, Math500, and ReasonOrderQA. Orange bars show Answer-First accuracy; blue portions show additional gain from CoT-First. LLaDA exhibits strong order robustness with minimal CoT-First gain (+2% on GSM8K). Dream, despite being a diffusion model, shows weaker robustness (+46% gain), suggesting that distillation from AR models may preserve order-sensitive behavior. Qwen shows the largest gap (+67%), consistent with AR’s structural dependence on generation order.

sections.heading: 3 ReasonOrderQA Benchmark
sections.text: To systematically probe the relationship between generation order and reasoning dynamics, we introduce ReasonOrderQA , a controlled benchmark of 1,000 problems across four difficulty levels: D1 (24%), D2 (39%), D3 (26%), and D4 (11%). See Appendix B for construction details.

sections.heading: Limitations of Existing Benchmarks.
sections.text: Math500 and GSM8K are suboptimal for studying order robustness: (1) intermediate steps are opaque, flawed reasoning may still yield correct answers; (2) failure modes are conflated and errors could stem from order sensitivity or insufficient capacity; (3) difficulty gradients are weak, e.g. Math500 levels do not produce well-separated behavioral patterns.

sections.heading: Design Goals.
sections.text: ReasonOrderQA addresses these limitations with three design goals: (1) Separate retrieval from reasoning: we decouple the retrieval stage (finding hidden variables) from the reasoning stage (computing the formula), enabling independent evaluation—Retrieval F1 measures the fraction of secret keys that appear in the model’s output, while Reasoning Accuracy measures whether the final answer is correct; (2) Clear difficulty gradients: four difficulty levels (D1-D4) with explicitly increasing arithmetic complexity, ensuring observable behavioral differences; (3) Verify early convergence for simple tasks: by including trivially simple problems (D1), we can test whether high-confidence tokens indeed converge earlier, validating the confidence-to-order mechanism.

sections.heading: Benchmark Construction.
sections.text: As illustrated in Figure 2 , we embed hidden variable definitions (e.g., “The secret key X is 7”) within a noisy context filled with distractors. The model must first retrieve these keys and then apply them to an arithmetic formula. We define four difficulty levels based on arithmetic complexity: • D1: X + Y + Z X+Y+Z (simple addition) • D2: X + Y − Z X+Y-Z (mixed operations) • D3: ( X + Y ) × Z (X+Y)\times Z (parentheses) • D4: ( X − Y × Z ) × W (X-Y\times Z)\times W (nested operations) Each level uses a fixed formula template while numeric values and distractor contexts vary across instances. This setup allows us to track, at each diffusion step, when the model retrieves variables (Retrieval F1) versus when it resolves the final answer (Reasoning Accuracy).

sections.heading: 4 Robustness to Controlled Order
sections.text: This section establishes an empirical baseline for order robustness by comparing autoregressive and diffusion-based models under different output ordering conditions.

sections.heading: Experimental Protocol.
sections.text: We compare three models representing different training paradigms: LLaDA-8B-Instruct, a masked diffusion language model trained from scratch ( Nie et al., 2025 ) ; Dream-7B, a diffusion model distilled from autoregressive weights ( Ye et al., 2025 ) ; and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct ( Yang et al., 2024 ) , a standard autoregressive model. This comparison allows us to examine whether order robustness stems from the diffusion architecture itself or from training methodology. For diffusion models, we employ the default low-confidence remasking strategy (as described in § 2 ), which prioritizes tokens based on confidence rather than textual position. We evaluate all models on GSM8K, Math500, and ReasonOrderQA under both the standard CoT-First order and the adversarial Answer-First constraint. As illustrated in Figure 3 , LLaDA exhibits strong order robustness across all three datasets, with accuracy gaps between CoT-First and Answer-First consistently under 15%. In contrast, Qwen shows substantial order sensitivity, with gaps reaching 22-67%. The Dream experiment reveals a key insight. Despite being a diffusion model, Dream shows intermediate behavior with gaps of +46% (GSM8K), +11% (Math500), and +16% (ReasonOrderQA). Dream is distilled from an autoregressive model, and we account this to its intermediate performance. This suggests that order robustness is not an automatic property of diffusion architectures, but also depends on training methodology. Models distilled from AR may inherit order-sensitive representations, partially preserving the coupling between generation order and reasoning order. Figure 4 : Convergence trajectories on GSM8K. Blue and orange lines show LLaDA Diffusion under CoT-First and Answer-First prompting, respectively; gray dashed line shows Qwen2.5-7B final accuracy under Answer-First. Diffusion trajectories overlap almost perfectly regardless of output order, gradually improving to ∼ \sim 55% accuracy. The Qwen baseline achieves only ∼ \sim 23% under Answer-First, confirming the AR model’s order sensitivity. Figure 4 further validates this through inference-time dynamics: LLaDA’s trajectories overlap regardless of output order, while Qwen degrades substantially. We observe consistent patterns on Math500 (Appendix C ).

sections.heading: 5 Source of Order Robustness
sections.text: Having established the phenomenon, we now analyze the underlying patterns. Prior work has used token-level confidence in autoregressive LMs for uncertainty quantification ( Fadeeva et al., 2024 ; Malinin and Gales, 2021 ) and adaptive computation such as early-exiting ( Schuster et al., 2021 ; Bae et al., 2023 ) . However, in AR models, confidence remains a diagnostic signal : it does not alter the fixed left-to-right generation order. In diffusion models, this changes fundamentally i.e. confidence directly controls which tokens get unmasked next, turning it into a generation mechanism . We investigate whether token confidence correlates with task complexity. If harder tokens exhibit systematically lower confidence, the sampling algorithm would naturally defer them, creating an implicit complexity-based ordering regardless of textual position. Our analysis documents this empirical pattern across controlled difficulty levels.

sections.heading: Methodology.
sections.text: ReasonOrderQA provides an ideal testbed because its difficulty levels (D1-D4) directly manipulate answer token complexity: D1 requires simple addition, while D4 requires nested operations with operator precedence. We track two quantities: (1) token confidence: the probability assigned to the predicted token at each diffusion step, and (2) exposure timing: the step at which all answer tokens are unmasked. The structured output template (Answer: / Reasoning: / Retrieval:) provides natural delimiters for tracking each segment.

sections.heading: 5.1 Task Complexity Reflects in Confidence
sections.text: Figure 5 : Answer token confidence decreases with problem difficulty. For each problem, we compute the mean confidence across all diffusion steps for answer tokens (located via the “Answer:” delimiter). Each box shows the distribution across problems within that difficulty level. D1 exhibits the highest mean confidence ( ∼ \sim 0.99), while D4 shows the lowest ( ∼ \sim 0.55). Variance also increases with difficulty. See Figure 11 for Math500 results. Figure 5 shows that answer token confidence decreases monotonically with task difficulty. For simple addition (D1), the model achieves near-perfect confidence ( ∼ \sim 0.99), indicating that the answer can be resolved almost immediately. As arithmetic complexity increases through D2-D4, confidence drops progressively, reaching only ∼ \sim 0.55 for the most complex nested operations (D4). See Appendix D for step-by-step confidence trajectory visualizations. Beyond mean confidence, the variance pattern is equally informative. D1-D2 problems cluster tightly around their means, suggesting consistent difficulty across instances. In contrast, D3-D4 exhibit substantial spread, reflecting that some problems within these levels are tractable while others remain challenging. This variance increase indicates that the model’s confidence is sensitive not only to the formula structure but also to the specific numeric values involved. This relationship between task complexity and confidence has a direct implication for generation order: since the sampling algorithm unmasks high-confidence tokens first, simpler answer tokens will be exposed earlier than complex ones, regardless of their textual position. We verify this prediction in the next subsection.

sections.heading: 5.2 Harder Tokens Unmask Later

Right (D4): Answer tokens remain low confidence (blue/green) until ∼ \sim 200 steps, while many other tokens also show delayed convergence. First, harder tasks produce more low-confidence tokens overall: in D1, most tokens converge quickly (bottom panel shows predominantly yellow), while D4 reveals many more low-confidence tokens (blue/green regions) across the entire generation. sections.heading: 5.3 Complexity-Based Ordering Enables Correctness
sections.text: The previous subsections document a consistent empirical pattern: task complexity correlates with token confidence, and low-confidence tokens are deferred by the sampling algorithm. This complexity-correlated ordering appears to enable order robustness. By deferring complex answer tokens, the model gains sufficient refinement time to resolve them correctly, regardless of their textual position. Figure 7 provides evidence for this pattern. Correct answers follow expected exposure timing, while wrong answers deviate. In D1-D2, both correct and wrong answers cluster at low exposure steps, as the tasks are simple enough to resolve quickly. However, in D3, correct answers maintain a consistent exposure distribution (mean ∼ \sim 30 steps), while wrong answers show higher variance and more extreme values. In D4, where only one answer is correct, that single success has a notably lower exposure step than the failures. This reveals why diffusion models achieve order robustness: confidence-based remasking implicitly prioritizes reasoning before answer commitment by delaying complex tokens until sufficient refinement occurs. This pattern holds when complexity differences are clear (D3), it breaks down when tokens are exposed too early (premature commitment) or the model never reaches sufficient confidence (D4). This explains both the robustness observed in § 4 and sets up our investigation of breakdown conditions in the next section. We provide an information-theoretic formalization connecting this mechanism to recent analyses of parallel decoding in Appendix G.3 .

sections.heading: 6 When Order Robustness Breaks Down
sections.text: The evidence in § 5 suggests that token ordering correlates with relative complexity, but when does this pattern break down? We identify two key factors: (1) insufficient complexity differences between tokens, and (2) large generation lengths. Using ReasonOrderQA under the Answer-First setting, we test these factors by tracking the temporal relationship between retrieval, reasoning, and answer tokens. Figure 8 : Mean Accuracy under Answer-First across difficulty levels. Left: early-stage dynamics (steps 0-20). Right: full trajectory (steps 0-200). Stars mark the step at which retrieval accuracy reaches 0.95, indicating when the model has internally identified the relevant variables. D1 converges quickly; D2 and D3 show gradual improvement; D4 remains near zero ( ∼ \sim 1%, 1/109 correct) as the task exceeds model capacity.

sections.heading: 6.1 Breakdown Condition 1: Insufficient Complexity Differences
sections.text: Figure 8 shows how accuracy evolves during Answer-First generation. We observe that order robustness breaks down when tokens have similar complexity levels. The contrast between D 2 D_{2} and D 3 D_{3} is particularly revealing. In D 2 D_{2} (mixed addition/subtraction), accuracy plateaus early at ∼ \sim 55% and shows minimal improvement after step 20. The answer tokens ( X + Y − Z X+Y-Z ) and retrieval tokens (finding X, Y, Z values) have similar complexity, so the model cannot reliably distinguish which to decode first. This leads to early commitment that results in errors that cannot be corrected in later steps. In contrast, D 3 D_{3} (parenthesized multiplication) demonstrates successful robustness: accuracy continues rising from ∼ \sim 25% at step 20 to ∼ \sim 35% at convergence. The stars in Figure 8 mark when retrieval converges (0.95 F1); crucially, D 3 D_{3} shows substantial post-retrieval accuracy growth after this point, while D 2 D_{2} has already plateaued. This indicates that D 3 D_{3} ’s retrieval tokens require only pattern matching while its answer tokens require multi-step computation, creating a complexity gap that allows the model to correctly prioritize retrieval before committing to the answer. Notably, D 4 D_{4} shows a different pattern: it remains near zero ( ∼ \sim 1%) throughout, indicating that D 4 D_{4} exceeds the model’s reasoning capacity, implying that the task itself is too difficult regardless of ordering. D 1 D_{1} converges almost immediately to near-perfect accuracy ( > > 95%), confirming that simple tasks pose no ordering challenge. This finding reveals that complexity differences between tokens within the same problem, not problem-level complexity, determine when robustness breaks down.

sections.heading: The Generation Length Trade-off.
sections.text: LLaDA requires specifying the maximum generation length upfront, yet our findings show that larger lengths degrade order robustness. This creates a dilemma: complex problems requiring longer CoT reasoning need larger generation lengths, but this very increase undermines the model’s ability to distinguish token complexity. Resolving this, either through adaptive or block-wise generation is a promising direction for future work.

sections.heading: 6.3 Impact of Sampling Strategies
sections.text: Our analysis above uses the low-confidence remasking strategy, which prioritizes high-confidence tokens for unmasking. How do different sampling strategies affect order robustness? We evaluate multiple strategies (detailed in Appendix E ) under both CoT-First and Answer-First conditions on ReasonOrderQA. Among diffusion strategies, topk_margin achieves the highest Answer-First accuracy (60.0%), while entropy achieves the best order robustness (-9.8% relative). First, all diffusion strategies substantially outperform the AR baseline in order robustness: Qwen2.5-7B achieves the highest CoT-First accuracy (91.8%) but shows a substantial 68% relative drop under Answer-First prompting, while all diffusion strategies show much smaller drops (9.8%-26.3%). Second, Answer-First accuracy reveals a clear hierarchy based on the information used for unmasking: left_to_right achieves only 47.2%, random reaches 51.1%, while uncertainty-based strategies progressively improve entropy (54.5%), low_confidence (57.3%), and topk_margin (60.0%). This hierarchy reveals a key insight: uncertainty-based strategies all derive their signal from the same source i.e. the token probability distribution whether summarized as top-1 confidence, full-distribution entropy, or top-1 vs. top-2 margin. Access to this distributional information is what enables order robustness. The variation among uncertainty-based methods reflects a secondary accuracy-robustness trade-off: aggressive unmasking ( topk_margin ) achieves higher accuracy but risks premature commitment, while conservative strategies ( entropy ) preserve flexibility at the cost of absolute performance.

sections.heading: 7 Related Work
sections.text: We situate our work at the intersection of generation paradigms, diffusion models, and reasoning mechanisms.

sections.heading: Sequential vs. Parallel Generation.
sections.text: Autoregressive (AR) models generate tokens strictly left-to-right, creating a structural bias that limits global planning ( Vaswani et al., 2017 ; Brown et al., 2020 ) . This constraint causes failures in non-monotonic tasks and bidirectional reasoning, such as the reversal curse ( Berglund et al., 2023 ; Welleck et al., 2019 ) . Non-autoregressive (NAR) approaches attempt to break this linearity through parallel decoding ( Gu et al., 2017 ) , iterative refinement ( Lee et al., 2018 ; Ghazvininejad et al., 2019 ) , or insertion-based strategies ( Gu et al., 2019 ; Chan et al., 2020 ) . These methods, however, typically operate within fixed windows and do not fundamentally decouple reasoning order from generation order.

sections.heading: Diffusion Models for Text.
sections.text: Diffusion models introduce a parallel denoising paradigm ( Austin et al., 2021 ; Li et al., 2022 ) . Recent work has scaled this approach to large language models (LLMs) via discrete or masked diffusion ( Lou et al., 2024 ; Shi et al., 2024 ; Nie et al., 2024 ; Sahoo et al., 2024 ) , with LLaDA ( Nie et al., 2025 ) achieving state-of-the-art performance. While some studies explore adaptation from AR weights ( Gong et al., 2025 ; Gulrajani and Hashimoto, 2023 ) or block-wise generation ( Arriola et al., 2025 ) , most focus on final output quality ( Yi et al., 2024 ) . Our work differs by probing the internal dynamics of generation to reveal how order invariance emerges.

sections.heading: Order Robustness and Reasoning.
sections.text: Prior work examines the reversal curse ( Berglund et al., 2023 ) , non-monotonic generation ( Welleck et al., 2019 ) , and chain-of-thought robustness under noise ( Zhou et al., 2024 ; Wang et al., 2025a ) . Recent work by Chen et al. (2025) formalizes the Parallel-Sequential Contradiction (PSC), showing that DLLMs may revert to autoregressive-like behavior as task complexity increases. Our work offers a complementary perspective: confidence-based remasking can leverage token dependencies to achieve order-invariant reasoning.

sections.heading: 8 Conclusion
sections.text: We show that masked diffusion language models exhibit order robustness: unlike AR models that degrade substantially under Answer-First prompting (up to 67% relative drop), diffusion models trained from scratch remain stable ( ≤ \leq 4% relative drop). The underlying mechanism is complexity-based ordering where confidence-based sampling defers complex tokens until sufficient refinement occurs. Through ReasonOrderQA, we identify two breakdown conditions: insufficient complexity differences between tokens, and large generation lengths. In the ongoing debate between autoregressive and diffusion language models, we identify a scenario where diffusion-style generation is preferable: when the required output order conflicts with the model’s natural reasoning order. This provides a criterion for model selection and a design signal for future architectures aiming to balance instruction-following with accurate reasoning.

sections.heading: Appendix B ReasonOrderQA Dataset Construction
sections.text: We describe the generation procedure for ReasonOrderQA, a controlled benchmark designed to probe the relationship between generation order and reasoning dynamics. The dataset contains 1,000 problems with an approximate target passage length of 1,000 tokens per problem.

sections.heading: B.1 Difficulty Sampling
sections.text: Problems are sampled according to the distribution: D1:D2:D3:D4 = 0.25:0.40:0.25:0.10. This ensures coverage across all complexity levels while reflecting the natural distribution where moderate-difficulty problems (D2) are most common.

sections.heading: B.2 Expression Generation
sections.text: Each difficulty level uses a fixed arithmetic expression template with randomly sampled integers: • D1: X + Y + Z X+Y+Z where X , Y , Z ∈ [ 1 , 20 ] X,Y,Z\in[1,20] • D2: X + Y − Z X+Y-Z where X , Y , Z ∈ [ 1 , 50 ] X,Y,Z\in[1,50] • D3: ( X + Y ) × Z (X+Y)\times Z where X , Y , Z ∈ [ 1,100 ] X,Y,Z\in[1,100] • D4: ( X − Y × Z ) × W (X-Y\times Z)\times W where X , Y , Z , W ∈ [ 1,100 ] X,Y,Z,W\in[1,100] The gold answer is computed directly from the expression. D1-D2 use three variables, while D3-D4 introduce parentheses and D4 adds a fourth variable, creating strict complexity gradients.

sections.heading: B.3 Passage Generation
sections.text: Each problem includes a passage of approximately 1000 tokens that embeds the secret key values. The passage is constructed as follows: 1. Filler content: Random sentences are sampled from a pool of distractor sentences and filler fragments. Some sentences are extended with 3-8 additional fragment words to vary length. 2. Key insertion: Sentences containing the secret keys (e.g., “The secret key X is 42”) are randomly inserted into the passage at different positions. 3. Length normalization: Additional filler content is appended until the passage reaches the target length (1000 tokens). This design ensures that key retrieval requires scanning the entire passage rather than relying on positional heuristics.

sections.heading: B.4 Retrieval F1 Computation
sections.text: Retrieval F1 measures the fraction of ground-truth secret keys that appear in the model’s output. For ReasonOrderQA, each problem has a set of gold keys 𝒦 = { k 1 , k 2 , … , k n } \mathcal{K}=\{k_{1},k_{2},\ldots,k_{n}\} (where n = 3 n=3 for D1-D3 and n = 4 n=4 for D4).

sections.heading: Delimiter Detection.
sections.text: We detect the “Retrieval:” segment using string matching on the output text. The segment is defined as all text between the “Retrieval:” delimiter and either the next delimiter (“Reasoning:” or “Answer:”) or the end of the generation. For internal predictions (before tokens are committed), we apply the same procedure to the model’s predicted sequence 𝐱 ^ 0 ( t ) \hat{\mathbf{x}}_{0}^{(t)} at each diffusion step t t .

sections.heading: Key Extraction.
sections.text: From the detected retrieval segment, we extract all integers using regular expression matching ( \ \backslash d+ ). Let 𝒫 \mathcal{P} denote the set of extracted integers from the model’s output.

sections.heading: F1 Calculation.
sections.text: We compute precision, recall, and F1 as follows: Precision = | 𝒫 ∩ 𝒦 | | 𝒫 | , Recall = | 𝒫 ∩ 𝒦 | | 𝒦 | \displaystyle=\frac{|\mathcal{P}\cap\mathcal{K}|}{|\mathcal{P}|},\quad\text{Recall}=\frac{|\mathcal{P}\cap\mathcal{K}|}{|\mathcal{K}|} (2) F1 = 2 ⋅ Precision ⋅ Recall Precision + Recall \displaystyle=\frac{2\cdot\text{Precision}\cdot\text{Recall}}{\text{Precision}+\text{Recall}} (3) When | 𝒫 | = 0 |\mathcal{P}|=0 (no integers extracted), we set Precision = 0 =0 and F1 = 0 =0 .

sections.heading: Handling Partial Matches.
sections.text: We use exact integer matching: a predicted key matches a gold key if and only if they are numerically identical. Order is not considered, and we treat both 𝒫 \mathcal{P} and 𝒦 \mathcal{K} as sets. Duplicate predictions are counted only once (i.e., predicting the same key twice does not inflate precision).

sections.heading: B.5 Reasoning Accuracy
sections.text: Reasoning Accuracy is a binary metric: 1 if the model’s final answer exactly matches the gold answer, 0 otherwise. The answer is extracted from the “Answer:” segment using the same delimiter detection procedure. For answers wrapped in \boxed{} , we extract the content inside the box.

sections.heading: B.6 Exposure Timing
sections.text: The exposure step for a segment (Answer, Reasoning, or Retrieval) is defined as the first diffusion step t t at which all token positions within that segment are unmasked (i.e., no mask tokens remain in the segment). We detect segment boundaries using the delimiter tokens and track the mask status of each position across diffusion steps.

sections.text: To complement the aggregated confidence statistics in Figure 5 , we visualize how answer token confidence evolves across diffusion steps, separated by correctness. Figure 12 : Answer token confidence trajectories on ReasonOrderQA by difficulty level. Green lines show problems with correct answers; red lines show incorrect answers. Shaded regions indicate standard deviation. In D1 (acc=99%), both correct and wrong cases rapidly converge to high confidence. In D2-D3, correct answers (green) achieve higher confidence earlier than wrong answers (red), suggesting that confidence trajectory shape correlates with answer correctness. sections.heading: Appendix E Mathematical Formulation of Decoding Strategies
sections.text: To clarify the distinction between different decoding strategies used in our experiments, we provide a formal mathematical characterization of three decoding paradigms: pure autoregressive decoding, LLaDA diffusion decoding, and left_to_right decoding.

sections.heading: E.1 Pure Autoregressive Decoding
sections.text: In a standard autoregressive language model, generation follows a strict left-to-right factorization: p AR ​ ( 𝐱 ) = ∏ i = 1 L p ⁡ ( x i ∣ x < i ) p_{\text{AR}}(\mathbf{x})=\prod_{i=1}^{L}p(x_{i}\mid x_{<i}) (4) During inference, tokens are generated sequentially: x i ∼ p ( x i ∣ x < i ) , i = 1 , 2 , … , L x_{i}\sim p(x_{i}\mid x_{<i}),\quad i=1,2,\ldots,L (5) At each step i i , the model can only condition on previously generated tokens x < i = [ x 1 , … , x i − 1 ] x_{<i}=[x_{1},\ldots,x_{i-1}] . This creates a structural constraint: token x i x_{i} cannot access information from future positions x > i x_{>i} .

sections.heading: E.2 LLaDA Diffusion Decoding
sections.text: LLaDA diffusion decoding uses a bidirectional mask predictor that estimates the entire sequence at each timestep. The generative process is: p θ ( 𝐱 0 ) = ∫ p ( 𝐱 T ) ∏ t = 1 T p θ ( 𝐱 t − 1 ∣ 𝐱 t ) d 𝐱 1 : T p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{0})=\int p(\mathbf{x}_{T})\prod_{t=1}^{T}p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{t-1}\mid\mathbf{x}_{t})d\mathbf{x}_{1:T} (6) where 𝐱 T \mathbf{x}_{T} is a fully masked sequence, and the reverse process iteratively denoises: 𝐱 ^ 0 ( t ) = p θ ( ⋅ ∣ 𝐱 t ) \hat{\mathbf{x}}_{0}^{(t)}=p_{\theta}(\cdot\mid\mathbf{x}_{t}) (7) The mask predictor p θ ( ⋅ ∣ 𝐱 t ) p_{\theta}(\cdot\mid\mathbf{x}_{t}) is a bidirectional Transformer that simultaneously predicts all masked tokens: 𝐱 ^ 0 ( t ) ​ [ j ] = p θ ​ ( x j ∣ 𝐱 t ) , ∀ j ∈ { 1 , … , L } \hat{\mathbf{x}}_{0}^{(t)}[j]=p_{\theta}(x_{j}\mid\mathbf{x}_{t}),\quad\forall j\in\{1,\ldots,L\} (8) where 𝐱 t \mathbf{x}_{t} contains both masked and unmasked tokens, and the bidirectional attention allows each position to attend to all other positions. The default strategy for LLaDA is low_confidence remasking ( Nie et al., 2025 ) , which selects tokens to unmask based on confidence scores: unmask ​ ( 𝐱 t , 𝐱 ^ 0 ( t ) ) = { j : conf ​ ( 𝐱 ^ 0 ( t ) ​ [ j ] ) > τ t } , where conf j = max v ∈ 𝒱 ⁡ p θ ​ ( x j = v ∣ 𝐱 t ) \text{unmask}(\mathbf{x}_{t},\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{0}^{(t)})=\{j:\text{conf}(\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{0}^{(t)}[j])>\tau_{t}\},\quad\text{where }\text{conf}_{j}=\max_{v\in\mathcal{V}}p_{\theta}(x_{j}=v\mid\mathbf{x}_{t}) (9) where τ t \tau_{t} is a threshold that determines how many tokens to unmask at step t t . This allows tokens to be unmasked in any order based on their inferential certainty, not their textual position.

sections.heading: E.3 Alternative Unmasking Strategies
sections.text: Beyond low_confidence , we evaluate several alternative strategies that differ in how they prioritize tokens: • topk_margin ( Kim et al., 2025 ) : Unmasks tokens based on the margin between top-1 and top-2 probabilities: margin j = p j ( 1 ) − p j ( 2 ) \text{margin}_{j}=p^{(1)}_{j}-p^{(2)}_{j} . A larger margin indicates higher decisiveness. • entropy : Unmasks tokens with lowest entropy: H j = − ∑ v p θ ( x j = v ∣ 𝐱 t ) log p θ ( x j = v ∣ 𝐱 t ) H_{j}=-\sum_{v}p_{\theta}(x_{j}=v\mid\mathbf{x}_{t})\log p_{\theta}(x_{j}=v\mid\mathbf{x}_{t}) . Unlike low_confidence , this considers the full distribution shape. • random ( Austin et al., 2021 ) : Unmasks tokens uniformly at random, serving as a baseline without confidence-based selection.

sections.heading: E.4 Left-to-Right Decoding
sections.text: ( left_to_right ) The left_to_right strategy uses the same bidirectional mask predictor p θ ( ⋅ ∣ 𝐱 t ) p_{\theta}(\cdot\mid\mathbf{x}_{t}) as LLaDA diffusion, but enforces a strict left-to-right unmasking schedule. Crucially, the model still computes predictions for all tokens at each step: 𝐱 ^ 0 ( t ) = p θ ( ⋅ ∣ 𝐱 t ) , 𝐱 ^ 0 ( t ) [ j ] = p θ ( x j ∣ 𝐱 t ) , ∀ j \hat{\mathbf{x}}_{0}^{(t)}=p_{\theta}(\cdot\mid\mathbf{x}_{t}),\quad\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{0}^{(t)}[j]=p_{\theta}(x_{j}\mid\mathbf{x}_{t}),\quad\forall j (10) The unmasking strategy, however, is constrained to follow an autoregressive order: unmask AR ​ ( 𝐱 t , 𝐱 ^ 0 ( t ) ) = { j : j ≤ i t } \text{unmask}_{\text{AR}}(\mathbf{x}_{t},\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{0}^{(t)})=\{j:j\leq i_{t}\} (11) where i t i_{t} is the current leftmost masked position. This means: • The model computes predictions for all positions (using bidirectional attention) • But only unmasks tokens in strict left-to-right order • The underlying parameterization remains diffusion-based, not AR-based This formulation clarifies that left_to_right is not a true autoregressive model, but rather a diffusion model with an AR-like unmasking schedule. The bidirectional computation allows it to access future context internally, even though tokens are unmasked sequentially. This distinction is crucial for understanding why left_to_right may still exhibit some robustness compared to pure AR models, while being more constrained than full diffusion decoding.

sections.heading: Appendix F Prompt Templates
sections.text: To evaluate order robustness, we employ two distinct prompt templates that strictly enforce output formatting. The first enforces the conventional reasoning-first structure, while the second imposes an adversarial answer-first constraint.

sections.heading: F.1 Standard Chain-of-Thought Prompt
sections.text: This prompt instructs the model to generate the reasoning trace prior to the final numerical result, adhering to the standard causal generation order. Explain the solution with a careful chain-of-thought before giving the final numeric result, and report the final answer inside \boxed{} . You MUST output your answer in the following exact structure: Reasoning: (explain how you combined the numbers to obtain the final result) Answer: \boxed{number}

sections.heading: F.2 Answer-First Adversarial Prompt
sections.text: This prompt inverts the generation order, requiring the model to commit to a final answer before articulating the supporting logic. You MUST start the response with the literal text "Answer:" on its own line (no text before it). Immediately after the heading, output the numeric answer wrapped in \boxed{} . sections.heading: Appendix G Mathematical Analysis of Confidence and Complexity
sections.text: We provide formal definitions of confidence, uncertainty, and difficulty to support the mechanistic analysis in § 5 .

sections.heading: G.1 Formal Definitions
sections.text: At each diffusion step t t , the mask predictor p θ ( ⋅ ∣ 𝐱 t ) p_{\theta}(\cdot\mid\mathbf{x}_{t}) produces a probability distribution over the vocabulary for each position j ∈ { 1 , … , L gen } j\in\{1,\ldots,L_{\text{gen}}\} . We define: • Confidence for token j j at step t t : c j ( t ) = max v ∈ 𝒱 ⁡ p θ ​ ( x j = v ∣ 𝐱 t ) c_{j}^{(t)}=\max_{v\in\mathcal{V}}p_{\theta}(x_{j}=v\mid\mathbf{x}_{t}) (12) where 𝒱 \mathcal{V} is the vocabulary. This represents the model’s certainty about the most likely token at position j j . • Uncertainty for token j j at step t t (measured as entropy): H j ( t ) = − ∑ v ∈ 𝒱 p θ ( x j = v ∣ 𝐱 t ) log p θ ( x j = v ∣ 𝐱 t ) H_{j}^{(t)}=-\sum_{v\in\mathcal{V}}p_{\theta}(x_{j}=v\mid\mathbf{x}_{t})\log p_{\theta}(x_{j}=v\mid\mathbf{x}_{t}) (13) Higher entropy indicates greater uncertainty about the token’s identity. • Difficulty for token j j : We define difficulty as the number of diffusion steps required to achieve high confidence. A token is ”difficult” if it requires more steps to converge: d j = arg min t { c j ( t ) > τ } d_{j}=\arg\min_{t}\{c_{j}^{(t)}>\tau\} (14) where τ \tau is a confidence threshold (e.g., 0.9). Smaller values of d j d_{j} indicate tokens that converge early (easy), while larger values indicate tokens that converge late or never (hard). If a token never reaches the threshold, we set d j = T + 1 d_{j}=T+1 to indicate maximum difficulty. This notion of difficulty is schedule-dependent and reflects convergence behavior under the specific remasking strategy used in our experiments.

sections.heading: G.2 Relative Complexity Judgment
sections.text: The model’s ability to judge relative complexity between tokens i i and j j depends on its capacity to distinguish their confidence distributions. We define the confidence separation at step t t as: Δ i ​ j ( t ) = | c i ( t ) − c j ( t ) | \Delta_{ij}^{(t)}=|c_{i}^{(t)}-c_{j}^{(t)}| (15) When Δ i ​ j ( t ) \Delta_{ij}^{(t)} is large, the model can reliably determine which token should be decoded first. When Δ i ​ j ( t ) \Delta_{ij}^{(t)} is small (tokens have similar confidence), the model struggles to prioritize. The confidence landscape variance across all tokens at step t t is: σ c ( t ) = 1 L gen ​ ∑ j = 1 L gen ( c j ( t ) − c ¯ ( t ) ) 2 \sigma_{c}^{(t)}=\sqrt{\frac{1}{L_{\text{gen}}}\sum_{j=1}^{L_{\text{gen}}}(c_{j}^{(t)}-\bar{c}^{(t)})^{2}} (16) where c ¯ ( t ) = 1 L gen ​ ∑ j = 1 L gen c j ( t ) \bar{c}^{(t)}=\frac{1}{L_{\text{gen}}}\sum_{j=1}^{L_{\text{gen}}}c_{j}^{(t)} is the mean confidence. This variance measure complements the pairwise separation Δ i ​ j ( t ) \Delta_{ij}^{(t)} : low variance indicates a flat confidence landscape where the model struggles to prioritize tokens i.e. the key factor underlying the breakdown condition identified in § 6.1 .

sections.heading: G.3 Connection to Information-Theoretic Analysis of Parallel Decoding
sections.text: Our empirical findings on complexity-based ordering can be connected to recent information-theoretic analyses of parallel decoding in diffusion language models ( Kang et al., 2025 ) .

sections.heading: Conditional Total Correlation as a Measure of Parallel Decoding Difficulty.
sections.text: Kang et al. (2025) show that the minimum achievable KL divergence for parallel decoding is lower-bounded by the conditional total correlation: min θ D KL ( P data ( Y | X ) ∥ P θ ( Y | X ) ) ≥ C ( Y | X ) , \min_{\theta}D_{\text{KL}}(P_{\text{data}}(Y|X)\|P_{\theta}(Y|X))\geq C(Y|X), (17) where C ⁡ ( Y | X ) = ∑ i H ⁡ ( y i | X ) − H ⁡ ( Y | X ) C(Y|X)=\sum_{i}H(y_{i}|X)-H(Y|X) measures the total token dependencies. When C ⁡ ( Y | X ) > 0 C(Y|X)>0 , parallel decoding inevitably incurs distribution error.

sections.heading: From Total Correlation to Entropy Gap.
sections.text: While C ⁡ ( Y | X ) C(Y|X) characterizes whether parallel decoding will degrade quality, it does not directly explain when order robustness holds. We propose that order robustness depends on the entropy gap between token types rather than overall task complexity. For a task with answer tokens Y A Y_{A} and reasoning tokens Y R Y_{R} , define the entropy gap: Δ H = 𝔼 y ∈ Y A ​ [ H ⁡ ( y | X , S < y ) ] − 𝔼 y ∈ Y R ​ [ H ⁡ ( y | X , S < y ) ] , \Delta_{H}=\mathbb{E}_{y\in Y_{A}}[H(y|X,S_{<y})]-\mathbb{E}_{y\in Y_{R}}[H(y|X,S_{<y})], (18) where S < y S_{<y} denotes the tokens decoded before y y under a given remasking trajectory. Note that Δ H \Delta_{H} is defined with respect to the effective conditioning induced by the confidence-based remasking schedule; it characterizes the entropy gap along the actual decoding path rather than an abstract positional ordering.

sections.heading: Entropy Gap as a Proxy for Order Robustness.
sections.text: To connect entropy with our confidence-based analysis, we note that confidence can be viewed as a coarse proxy for normalized entropy. Under peaked distributions where top-1 probability mass dominates, confidence is inversely related to entropy: c j ( t ) ∝ 1 − H ⁡ ( y j | X , S < j ) log ⁡ | 𝒱 | . c_{j}^{(t)}\;\propto\;1-\frac{H(y_{j}|X,S_{<j})}{\log|\mathcal{V}|}. (19) We use this expression only to convey monotonic intuition rather than a quantitative identity. The relationship between softmax max-probability and entropy can diverge for multi-modal or flat-tailed distributions. Nevertheless, our empirically observed confidence separation Δ i ​ j ( t ) \Delta_{ij}^{(t)} provides a practical proxy for the entropy gap between tokens. This suggests a heuristic criterion for predicting order robustness: • Order robustness tends to hold when Δ H > ϵ \Delta_{H}>\epsilon for some task-dependent threshold ϵ > 0 \epsilon>0 : answer tokens exhibit sufficiently higher entropy than reasoning tokens, leading them to be deferred by confidence-based remasking. • Order robustness tends to break down when Δ H ≈ 0 \Delta_{H}\approx 0 : tokens have similar entropy, and the model cannot reliably distinguish decoding priority (our D 2 D_{2} scenario).

sections.heading: Complementary Perspectives.
sections.text: Our analysis offers an interpretive lens that complements Kang et al. (2025) : • Their result: C ⁡ ( Y | X ) > 0 C(Y|X)>0 establishes a lower bound showing that parallel decoding cannot eliminate errors arising from token dependencies in the worst case. • Our interpretation: When Δ H > 0 \Delta_{H}>0 , confidence-based remasking can exploit signals induced by these dependencies, potentially guiding the model toward correct reasoning order despite non-zero total correlation. We emphasize that this is an empirical observation rather than a formal guarantee: the lower bound of Kang et al. (2025) does not prescribe how diffusion samplers use dependencies, only that they cannot be ignored. Our findings suggest that token dependencies, while limiting parallel decoding in principle, can also induce uncertainty gradients that remasking-based schedules may exploit, though the precise conditions under which this occurs remain an open question.

Report Issue Back to Abstract Download PDF Contents Reading mode Colour theme License: CC BY 4.0 arXiv:2601.22035v1 [cs.CL] 29 Jan 2026 Thinking Out of Order: When Output Order Stops Reflecting Reasoning Order in Diffusion Language Models Longxuan Yu Affiliation: University of California, Riverside, CA, USA Yu Fu Affiliation: University of California, Riverside, CA, USA Shaorong Zhang Affiliation: University of California, Riverside, CA, USA Hui Liu Affiliation: Independent Researcher Mukund Varma T Affiliation: University of California, San Diego, CA, USA Greg Ver Steeg Affiliation: University of California, Riverside, CA, USA Yue Dong Affiliation: University of California, Riverside, CA, USA Correspondence to: yuedongle@gmail.com Abstract Autoregressive (AR) language models enforce a fixed left-to-right generation order, creating a fundamental limitation when the required output structure conflicts with natural reasoning (e.g., producing answers before explanations due to presentation or schema constraints). In such cases, AR models must commit to answers before generating intermediate reasoning, and this rigid constraint forces premature commitment. Masked diffusion language models (MDLMs), which iteratively refine all tokens in parallel, offer a way to decouple computation order from output structure. We validate this capability on GSM8K, Math500, and ReasonOrderQA, a benchmark we introduce with controlled difficulty and order-level evaluation. When prompts request answers before reasoning, AR models exhibit large accuracy gaps compared to standard chain-of-thought ordering (up to 67% relative drop), while MDLMs remain stable ( ≤ \leq 14% relative drop), a property we term order robustness . Using ReasonOrderQA, we present evidence that MDLMs achieve order robustness by stabilizing simpler tokens (e.g., reasoning steps) earlier in the diffusion process than complex ones (e.g., final answers), enabling reasoning tokens to stabilize before answer commitment. Finally, we identify failure conditions where this advantage weakens, outlining the limits required for order robustness. Keywords: Diffusion Language Models, Order Robustness, Chain-of-Thought Reasoning, Masked Diffusion † † affiliationnotice: Equal contribution † \dagger Equal advising. 1 Introduction Figure 1 : Masked Diffusion models reason before answering—even when asked to answer first. Under “answer-first” prompting, AR models must commit to answers before reasoning (generation order = output order). Masked diffusion LMs decode reasoning tokens first regardless of output position, enabling order robustness . Instruction-following is a fundamental capability of modern language models, enabling them to adhere to user-specified constraints on output format and structure ( Ouyang et al., 2022 ; Wei et al., 2021 ) . Chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting ( Kojima et al., 2022 ; Wei et al., 2022 ) extends this capability to complex reasoning tasks by instructing models to generate intermediate reasoning steps before producing final answers, significantly improving performance across diverse domains. However, this success depends on a critical assumption: the output order aligns with the model’s internal reasoning order. In practice, this assumption is often violated by deployment constraints that prioritize application needs, such as the Minto Pyramid principle ( Minto, 2009 ) mandating conclusions before arguments to optimize human comprehension, or JSON schemas ( Tam et al., 2024 ) enforcing fixed key sequences that force models to produce complex outputs (e.g., summary statistics) before the data needed to derive them. For autoregressive (AR) language models, this mismatch exposes a fundamental limitation of left-to-right generation. AR models factorize sequences strictly in temporal order ( Vaswani et al., 2017 ; Brown et al., 2020 ) , coupling the generation order (the sequence of probability assignments) with the output order (the sequence of emitted tokens). When answers must precede reasoning in the output, AR models are forced to commit to answer tokens before the intermediate reasoning tokens exist in the generated context. This premature commitment constrains the model’s ability to revise early predictions and has been shown to limit non-monotonic generation and bidirectional planning ( Welleck et al., 2019 ; Gu et al., 2019 ) . Yet its consequences for instruction-constrained reasoning remain largely unexplored. Masked diffusion language models (MDLMs) offer an alternative generation paradigm. Rather than producing tokens sequentially, MDLMs iteratively refine a full-length sequence using a bidirectional Transformer and a sampling procedure that determines which positions to finalize at each step ( Nie et al., 2025 ; Sahoo et al., 2024 ) . This process decouples computation order from textual position, allowing token estimates to evolve based on global sequence context and potentially enabling internal reasoning to emerge before answer commitment, even when answers appear first in the output. While recent work has primarily evaluated diffusion LMs in terms of final output quality and inference efficiency ( Wu et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2025b ) , their ability to support reliable reasoning under strict output-order constraints has not been systematically examined. To investigate this capability, we study order robustness , defined as the ability to maintain reasoning accuracy when the prompt-specified output order is reversed (CoT-First versus Answer-First). Across GSM8K, Math500, and a new benchmark we introduce, we uncover a striking contrast between generation paradigms. Under Answer-First prompting, Qwen ( Yang et al., 2024 ) (autoregressive) exhibits large relative accuracy drops (up to ∼ \sim 67%), whereas LLaDA ( Nie et al., 2025 ) (diffusion trained from scratch) remains largely stable with only a 4% relative drop. Dream ( Ye et al., 2025 ) , a diffusion model distilled from autoregressive weights, shows intermediate degradation ( ∼ \sim 46%), indicating that order robustness depends not only on architecture but also on training methodology. To make the underlying mechanism measurable rather than anecdotal, we introduce ReasonOrderQA , a controlled benchmark with graded arithmetic complexity (D1-D4) and explicit order-level evaluation. As illustrated in Figure 1 , we observe a consistent complexity-driven stabilization pattern in diffusion generation: lower-complexity reasoning tokens achieve high confidence and stabilize earlier than higher-complexity answer tokens, enabling internal reasoning to be refined before answer commitment regardless of output position. We further probe the boundaries of this mechanism and identify specific conditions under which order robustness breaks down. Our contributions: • We introduce ReasonOrderQA , a controlled benchmark with graded difficulty and order-level evaluation, enabling fine-grained analysis of order sensitivity across different token complexity levels. • Our detailed experiments provide evidence for order-robust reasoning in masked diffusion LMs: unlike AR models that degrade significantly under answer-first prompting, diffusion models maintain accuracy regardless of output order. • We systematically identify the mechanism for such order-robustness i.e. diffusion sampling automatically delays commitment on low-confidence tokens such as the final answers while high confidence tokens that convey reasoning stabilize earlier. • Finally, we identify failure cases where order robustness weakens, highlighting the limits of this implicit effect and identifying directions for reliable order-agnostic generation. 2 Preliminary We define order robustness as the ability to maintain reasoning accuracy when the prompt-specified output order is altered (e.g., CoT-First vs. Answer-First). Autoregressive Models. Autoregressive (AR) models factorize the joint probability of a sequence 𝐱 = [ x 1 , … , x L ] \mathbf{x}=[x_{1},\dots,x_{L}] as: p AR ​ ( 𝐱 ) = ∏ i = 1 L p ⁡ ( x i ∣ x < i ) p_{\text{AR}}(\mathbf{x})=\prod_{i=1}^{L}p(x_{i}\mid x_{<i}) (1) This enforces a strict left-to-right dependency: the prediction of token x i x_{i} can only attend to past context x < i x_{<i} , coupling generation order with textual position. Figure 2 : ReasonOrderQA benchmark design. Each problem contains (1) a noisy context with hidden variable definitions, (2) an arithmetic formula of varying complexity (D1-D4), and (3) evaluation under two generation orders (Standard: reasoning→answer, Reverse: answer→reasoning). This design decouples retrieval difficulty from reasoning complexity. Masked Diffusion Language Models. Masked diffusion LMs like LLaDA ( Nie et al., 2025 ) define a reverse process that recovers clean data from a fully masked sequence. A bidirectional Transformer predicts all masked tokens simultaneously, allowing the model to access global context at any step and theoretically decoupling generation order from textual position. Starting from a fully masked sequence at step t = T t=T , the model iteratively predicts 𝐱 ^ 0 \hat{\mathbf{x}}_{0} from 𝐱 t \mathbf{x}_{t} . At each diffusion step, high-confidence tokens are retained while low-confidence tokens are re-masked for refinement in subsequent steps (i.e., tokens with low confidence are “remasked”). This prioritizes high-certainty predictions globally, regardless of their position in the sequence. We use this as our default strategy throughout the paper; alternative strategies are compared in § 6.3 . Task Formulation and Metrics. To precisely analyze the generation dynamics, we formalize the task settings and define the terminology used throughout our experiments. We consider two output orders for a question x Q x_{Q} with rationale x R x_{R} and answer x A x_{A} . In the CoT-First setting, the model produces 𝐱 = [ x Q , x R , x A ] \mathbf{x}=[x_{Q},x_{R},x_{A}] , which matches the standard left-to-right reasoning narrative and the autoregressive training objective. In the Answer-First setting, the model is constrained to output 𝐱 = [ x Q , x A , x R ] \mathbf{x}=[x_{Q},x_{A},x_{R}] . The prompt templates enforcing these formats are provided in Appendix F . Generation Settings. We use generation length L = 256 L=256 and diffusion steps T = 256 T=256 . Because the model estimates the entire sequence at every step, we can track internal predictions separately from the completion text (tokens actually committed). Full settings are in Appendix A (Table 4 ). Figure 3 : Order robustness across diffusion and autoregressive models. We compare LLaDA (diffusion, trained from scratch), Dream (diffusion, distilled from AR), and Qwen (autoregressive) on GSM8K, Math500, and ReasonOrderQA. Orange bars show Answer-First accuracy; blue portions show additional gain from CoT-First. LLaDA exhibits strong order robustness with minimal CoT-First gain (+2% on GSM8K). Dream, despite being a diffusion model, shows weaker robustness (+46% gain), suggesting that distillation from AR models may preserve order-sensitive behavior. Qwen shows the largest gap (+67%), consistent with AR’s structural dependence on generation order. 3 ReasonOrderQA Benchmark To systematically probe the relationship between generation order and reasoning dynamics, we introduce ReasonOrderQA , a controlled benchmark of 1,000 problems across four difficulty levels: D1 (24%), D2 (39%), D3 (26%), and D4 (11%). See Appendix B for construction details. Limitations of Existing Benchmarks. Math500 and GSM8K are suboptimal for studying order robustness: (1) intermediate steps are opaque, flawed reasoning may still yield correct answers; (2) failure modes are conflated and errors could stem from order sensitivity or insufficient capacity; (3) difficulty gradients are weak, e.g. Math500 levels do not produce well-separated behavioral patterns. Design Goals. ReasonOrderQA addresses these limitations with three design goals: (1) Separate retrieval from reasoning: we decouple the retrieval stage (finding hidden variables) from the reasoning stage (computing the formula), enabling independent evaluation—Retrieval F1 measures the fraction of secret keys that appear in the model’s output, while Reasoning Accuracy measures whether the final answer is correct; (2) Clear difficulty gradients: four difficulty levels (D1-D4) with explicitly increasing arithmetic complexity, ensuring observable behavioral differences; (3) Verify early convergence for simple tasks: by including trivially simple problems (D1), we can test whether high-confidence tokens indeed converge earlier, validating the confidence-to-order mechanism. Benchmark Construction. As illustrated in Figure 2 , we embed hidden variable definitions (e.g., “The secret key X is 7”) within a noisy context filled with distractors. The model must first retrieve these keys and then apply them to an arithmetic formula. We define four difficulty levels based on arithmetic complexity: • D1: X + Y + Z X+Y+Z (simple addition) • D2: X + Y − Z X+Y-Z (mixed operations) • D3: ( X + Y ) × Z (X+Y)\times Z (parentheses) • D4: ( X − Y × Z ) × W (X-Y\times Z)\times W (nested operations) Each level uses a fixed formula template while numeric values and distractor contexts vary across instances. This setup allows us to track, at each diffusion step, when the model retrieves variables (Retrieval F1) versus when it resolves the final answer (Reasoning Accuracy). 4 Robustness to Controlled Order This section establishes an empirical baseline for order robustness by comparing autoregressive and diffusion-based models under different output ordering conditions. Experimental Protocol. We compare three models representing different training paradigms: LLaDA-8B-Instruct, a masked diffusion language model trained from scratch ( Nie et al., 2025 ) ; Dream-7B, a diffusion model distilled from autoregressive weights ( Ye et al., 2025 ) ; and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct ( Yang et al., 2024 ) , a standard autoregressive model. This comparison allows us to examine whether order robustness stems from the diffusion architecture itself or from training methodology. For diffusion models, we employ the default low-confidence remasking strategy (as described in § 2 ), which prioritizes tokens based on confidence rather than textual position. We evaluate all models on GSM8K, Math500, and ReasonOrderQA under both the standard CoT-First order and the adversarial Answer-First constraint. As illustrated in Figure 3 , LLaDA exhibits strong order robustness across all three datasets, with accuracy gaps between CoT-First and Answer-First consistently under 15%. In contrast, Qwen shows substantial order sensitivity, with gaps reaching 22-67%. The Dream experiment reveals a key insight. Despite being a diffusion model, Dream shows intermediate behavior with gaps of +46% (GSM8K), +11% (Math500), and +16% (ReasonOrderQA). Dream is distilled from an autoregressive model, and we account this to its intermediate performance. This suggests that order robustness is not an automatic property of diffusion architectures, but also depends on training methodology. Models distilled from AR may inherit order-sensitive representations, partially preserving the coupling between generation order and reasoning order. Figure 4 : Convergence trajectories on GSM8K. Blue and orange lines show LLaDA Diffusion under CoT-First and Answer-First prompting, respectively; gray dashed line shows Qwen2.5-7B final accuracy under Answer-First. Diffusion trajectories overlap almost perfectly regardless of output order, gradually improving to ∼ \sim 55% accuracy. The Qwen baseline achieves only ∼ \sim 23% under Answer-First, confirming the AR model’s order sensitivity. Figure 4 further validates this through inference-time dynamics: LLaDA’s trajectories overlap regardless of output order, while Qwen degrades substantially. We observe consistent patterns on Math500 (Appendix C ). 5 Source of Order Robustness Having established the phenomenon, we now analyze the underlying patterns. Prior work has used token-level confidence in autoregressive LMs for uncertainty quantification ( Fadeeva et al., 2024 ; Malinin and Gales, 2021 ) and adaptive computation such as early-exiting ( Schuster et al., 2021 ; Bae et al., 2023 ) . However, in AR models, confidence remains a diagnostic signal : it does not alter the fixed left-to-right generation order. In diffusion models, this changes fundamentally i.e. confidence directly controls which tokens get unmasked next, turning it into a generation mechanism . We investigate whether token confidence correlates with task complexity. If harder tokens exhibit systematically lower confidence, the sampling algorithm would naturally defer them, creating an implicit complexity-based ordering regardless of textual position. Our analysis documents this empirical pattern across controlled difficulty levels. Methodology. ReasonOrderQA provides an ideal testbed because its difficulty levels (D1-D4) directly manipulate answer token complexity: D1 requires simple addition, while D4 requires nested operations with operator precedence. We track two quantities: (1) token confidence: the probability assigned to the predicted token at each diffusion step, and (2) exposure timing: the step at which all answer tokens are unmasked. The structured output template (Answer: / Reasoning: / Retrieval:) provides natural delimiters for tracking each segment. 5.1 Task Complexity Reflects in Confidence Figure 5 : Answer token confidence decreases with problem difficulty. For each problem, we compute the mean confidence across all diffusion steps for answer tokens (located via the “Answer:” delimiter). Each box shows the distribution across problems within that difficulty level. D1 exhibits the highest mean confidence ( ∼ \sim 0.99), while D4 shows the lowest ( ∼ \sim 0.55). Variance also increases with difficulty. See Figure 11 for Math500 results. Figure 5 shows that answer token confidence decreases monotonically with task difficulty. For simple addition (D1), the model achieves near-perfect confidence ( ∼ \sim 0.99), indicating that the answer can be resolved almost immediately. As arithmetic complexity increases through D2-D4, confidence drops progressively, reaching only ∼ \sim 0.55 for the most complex nested operations (D4). See Appendix D for step-by-step confidence trajectory visualizations. Beyond mean confidence, the variance pattern is equally informative. D1-D2 problems cluster tightly around their means, suggesting consistent difficulty across instances. In contrast, D3-D4 exhibit substantial spread, reflecting that some problems within these levels are tractable while others remain challenging. This variance increase indicates that the model’s confidence is sensitive not only to the formula structure but also to the specific numeric values involved. This relationship between task complexity and confidence has a direct implication for generation order: since the sampling algorithm unmasks high-confidence tokens first, simpler answer tokens will be exposed earlier than complex ones, regardless of their textual position. We verify this prediction in the next subsection. 5.2 Harder Tokens Unmask Later Figure 6 : Confidence dynamics: D1 vs D4. Each heatmap shows token confidence (color) across diffusion steps (x-axis) and token positions (y-axis). Top row zooms into answer tokens (red box); bottom row shows all tokens. Left (D1): Answer tokens achieve high confidence (yellow) within ∼ \sim 10 steps. Right (D4): Answer tokens remain low confidence (blue/green) until ∼ \sim 200 steps, while many other tokens also show delayed convergence. Figure 6 reveals how confidence dynamics differ across difficulty levels. First, harder tasks produce more low-confidence tokens overall: in D1, most tokens converge quickly (bottom panel shows predominantly yellow), while D4 reveals many more low-confidence tokens (blue/green regions) across the entire generation. Second, since the sampling algorithm prioritizes high-confidence tokens for unmasking, these patterns directly determine exposure timing: in D1, the answer token region (red box) turns yellow early, so these tokens are unmasked quickly; in D4, the answer region remains blue/green for most of the trajectory, so the algorithm keeps selecting other high-confidence tokens first, delaying answer exposure until ∼ \sim 200 steps. To further understand how the sampling algorithm drives this behavior, we compare low_confidence (which prioritizes high-confidence tokens) against left_to_right (which forces LLaDA to unmask tokens strictly left-to-right while keeping the same model architecture; see Appendix E ). This comparison isolates the effect of sampling strategy. Table 1 quantifies this effect. The relationship is notably non-linear where, D1-D2 show relatively fast exposure (10-13 steps), but D3 jumps to 63.1 and D4 to 203.1 steps. The total Δ \Delta is +193.0 steps for low_confidence versus +3.4 for left_to_right (57 × \times difference), confirming that low-confidence tokens are delayed only when the sampling strategy allows confidence-based reordering. The exposure step is the first diffusion step at which all answer tokens are unmasked (i.e., no mask tokens remain in the answer region). Each point represents one problem; green indicates correct answers, red indicates wrong answers. Diamond markers show the mean exposure step for each group. As difficulty increases (D1 → \to D4), correct answers maintain consistent exposure timing patterns, while wrong answers exhibit increasingly scattered and extreme exposure steps. In D4, the single correct case (n=1) has notably lower exposure step than the wrong cases, suggesting that appropriate delay correlates with success. 5.3 Complexity-Based Ordering Enables Correctness The previous subsections document a consistent empirical pattern: task complexity correlates with token confidence, and low-confidence tokens are deferred by the sampling algorithm. This complexity-correlated ordering appears to enable order robustness. By deferring complex answer tokens, the model gains sufficient refinement time to resolve them correctly, regardless of their textual position. Figure 7 provides evidence for this pattern. Correct answers follow expected exposure timing, while wrong answers deviate. In D1-D2, both correct and wrong answers cluster at low exposure steps, as the tasks are simple enough to resolve quickly. However, in D3, correct answers maintain a consistent exposure distribution (mean ∼ \sim 30 steps), while wrong answers show higher variance and more extreme values. In D4, where only one answer is correct, that single success has a notably lower exposure step than the failures. This reveals why diffusion models achieve order robustness: confidence-based remasking implicitly prioritizes reasoning before answer commitment by delaying complex tokens until sufficient refinement occurs. This pattern holds when complexity differences are clear (D3), it breaks down when tokens are exposed too early (premature commitment) or the model never reaches sufficient confidence (D4). This explains both the robustness observed in § 4 and sets up our investigation of breakdown conditions in the next section. We provide an information-theoretic formalization connecting this mechanism to recent analyses of parallel decoding in Appendix G.3 . 6 When Order Robustness Breaks Down The evidence in § 5 suggests that token ordering correlates with relative complexity, but when does this pattern break down? We identify two key factors: (1) insufficient complexity differences between tokens, and (2) large generation lengths. Using ReasonOrderQA under the Answer-First setting, we test these factors by tracking the temporal relationship between retrieval, reasoning, and answer tokens. Figure 8 : Mean Accuracy under Answer-First across difficulty levels. Left: early-stage dynamics (steps 0-20). Right: full trajectory (steps 0-200). Stars mark the step at which retrieval accuracy reaches 0.95, indicating when the model has internally identified the relevant variables. D1 converges quickly; D2 and D3 show gradual improvement; D4 remains near zero ( ∼ \sim 1%, 1/109 correct) as the task exceeds model capacity. 6.1 Breakdown Condition 1: Insufficient Complexity Differences Figure 8 shows how accuracy evolves during Answer-First generation. We observe that order robustness breaks down when tokens have similar complexity levels. The contrast between D 2 D_{2} and D 3 D_{3} is particularly revealing. In D 2 D_{2} (mixed addition/subtraction), accuracy plateaus early at ∼ \sim 55% and shows minimal improvement after step 20. The answer tokens ( X + Y − Z X+Y-Z ) and retrieval tokens (finding X, Y, Z values) have similar complexity, so the model cannot reliably distinguish which to decode first. This leads to early commitment that results in errors that cannot be corrected in later steps. In contrast, D 3 D_{3} (parenthesized multiplication) demonstrates successful robustness: accuracy continues rising from ∼ \sim 25% at step 20 to ∼ \sim 35% at convergence. The stars in Figure 8 mark when retrieval converges (0.95 F1); crucially, D 3 D_{3} shows substantial post-retrieval accuracy growth after this point, while D 2 D_{2} has already plateaued. Sequential vs. Parallel Generation. Autoregressive (AR) models generate tokens strictly left-to-right, creating a structural bias that limits global planning ( Vaswani et al., 2017 ; Brown et al., 2020 ) . This constraint causes failures in non-monotonic tasks and bidirectional reasoning, such as the reversal curse ( Berglund et al., 2023 ; Welleck et al., 2019 ) . Non-autoregressive (NAR) approaches attempt to break this linearity through parallel decoding ( Gu et al., 2017 ) , iterative refinement ( Lee et al., 2018 ; Ghazvininejad et al., 2019 ) , or insertion-based strategies ( Gu et al., 2019 ; Chan et al., 2020 ) . These methods, however, typically operate within fixed windows and do not fundamentally decouple reasoning order from generation order. Diffusion Models for Text. Diffusion models introduce a parallel denoising paradigm ( Austin et al., 2021 ; Li et al., 2022 ) . Recent work has scaled this approach to large language models (LLMs) via discrete or masked diffusion ( Lou et al., 2024 ; Shi et al., 2024 ; Nie et al., 2024 ; Sahoo et al., 2024 ) , with LLaDA ( Nie et al., 2025 ) achieving state-of-the-art performance. While some studies explore adaptation from AR weights ( Gong et al., 2025 ; Gulrajani and Hashimoto, 2023 ) or block-wise generation ( Arriola et al., 2025 ) , most focus on final output quality ( Yi et al., 2024 ) . Our work differs by probing the internal dynamics of generation to reveal how order invariance emerges. Order Robustness and Reasoning. Prior work examines the reversal curse ( Berglund et al., 2023 ) , non-monotonic generation ( Welleck et al., 2019 ) , and chain-of-thought robustness under noise ( Zhou et al., 2024 ; Wang et al., 2025a ) . Recent work by Chen et al. (2025) formalizes the Parallel-Sequential Contradiction (PSC), showing that DLLMs may revert to autoregressive-like behavior as task complexity increases. Our work offers a complementary perspective: confidence-based remasking can leverage token dependencies to achieve order-invariant reasoning. 8 Conclusion We show that masked diffusion language models exhibit order robustness: unlike AR models that degrade substantially under Answer-First prompting (up to 67% relative drop), diffusion models trained from scratch remain stable ( ≤ \leq 4% relative drop). The underlying mechanism is complexity-based ordering where confidence-based sampling defers complex tokens until sufficient refinement occurs. Through ReasonOrderQA, we identify two breakdown conditions: insufficient complexity differences between tokens, and large generation lengths. In the ongoing debate between autoregressive and diffusion language models, we identify a scenario where diffusion-style generation is preferable: when the required output order conflicts with the model’s natural reasoning order. This provides a criterion for model selection and a design signal for future architectures aiming to balance instruction-following with accurate reasoning. B.1 Difficulty Sampling Problems are sampled according to the distribution: D1:D2:D3:D4 = 0.25:0.40:0.25:0.10. B.2 Expression Generation Each difficulty level uses a fixed arithmetic expression template with randomly sampled integers: • D1: X + Y + Z X+Y+Z where X , Y , Z ∈ [ 1 , 20 ] X,Y,Z\in[1,20] • D2: X + Y − Z X+Y-Z where X , Y , Z ∈ [ 1 , 50 ] X,Y,Z\in[1,50] • D3: ( X + Y ) × Z (X+Y)\times Z where X , Y , Z ∈ [ 1,100 ] X,Y,Z\in[1,100] • D4: ( X − Y × Z ) × W (X-Y\times Z)\times W where X , Y , Z , W ∈ [ 1,100 ] X,Y,Z,W\in[1,100] The gold answer is computed directly from the expression. B.3 Passage Generation Each problem includes a passage of approximately 1000 tokens that embeds the secret key values. The passage is constructed as follows: 1. Filler content: Random sentences are sampled from a pool of distractor sentences and filler fragments. Some sentences are extended with 3-8 additional fragment words to vary length. 2. Key insertion: Sentences containing the secret keys (e.g., “The secret key X is 42”) are randomly inserted into the passage at different positions. 3. Length normalization: Additional filler content is appended until the passage reaches the target length (1000 tokens). This design ensures that key retrieval requires scanning the entire passage rather than relying on positional heuristics. Appendix E Mathematical Formulation of Decoding Strategies To clarify the distinction between different decoding strategies used in our experiments, we provide a formal mathematical characterization of three decoding paradigms: pure autoregressive decoding, LLaDA diffusion decoding, and left_to_right decoding.
